# Inefficiency of Public Administration

## Problems and Dysfunctions of Public Administration, lecture at Universidad Francisco Marroquín, Guatemala, May 8, 2013. {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}
{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6F0TZGtyZE8 >}}
:::

Good morning. The EPRI^[Political Studies and International Relations Unit at Universidad Francisco Marroquín.] very kindly invited me to talk a bit about problems and dysfunctions of public administration, or something like that. They asked me to touch on that subject. It is a topic I enjoy addressing. I like to discuss the failure of the State, the failure of the public sector, and why it is difficult for public administrations to function well. So basically, we can start by analyzing what those failures are, what the root problems of public administration are, and then examine some of its malfunctions.

What does public administration do? What is the function of public administration? The function of public administration is the management of those socialist spheres of social life. That is to say, public administration appropriates—or the State appropriates. The State, to me, is an imaginary entity: it does not exist. If concrete, organized individuals do not exist, there is nothing called the State. In your head it may exist, through a map, through a series of things, the idea of Guatemala, Spain, Galicia, or the United States, but it has no real existence. It is a myth you hold in your brains. But anyway, that group of organized individuals who monopolize force decided that certain spheres of social life should be managed by those very individuals. There are spheres ceded to the market, and other spheres that they decide to administer or manage directly.

Thus, public administration is the management or administration of those parts of the economy that are socialist, of those parts of the economy that are socialized. For example, the State decides it will provide education: therefore, there is an educational administration. The State decides it will manage, say, the creation or monopoly of money: hence, there is a central bank and management of money. If the State decides it will administer and apply justice, then there is a public administration of justice. So those spheres of social life that the State administers, wholly or partially, are what we call public administration. A very pretty name, but basically it is this: the management of those spheres by that group of people who dominate the rest of society through force of arms.

What problem, or problems, does such management pose for us? Two, at first glance. One: the absence of economic calculation. Two: the lack of profit and loss. When we talk about the lack of profit and loss, I will delve a bit into the issue of economic calculation.

Have any of you played poker? Has no one here played a game of poker? No one. You played poker. Did you ever play with real money, and did you ever play without money? That is, with buttons, matches, or the like. Do you play the same way? Why not? Because when there is no money involved, when you are playing with buttons, the risk is lower. A very good definition. When the young lady plays poker with money, she directly bears the profits and bears the losses, yes or no? When playing with buttons, she bears neither profit nor loss. Well, there you have the difference between public management and private management. Cards are played differently, with different degrees of prudence, when there is profit and loss compared to when there is none. That is the difference between public administration and a strictly private enterprise: in one, you assume the profits and losses and play accordingly—you play prudently, you don't risk too much, or you risk only if you think you can win; in the other, you merely administer what is there and take no personal risk. If you sit down to play without money, you make all sorts of wild bets, you do all sorts of things. What does it matter? You start building pharaonic airports, you start launching all kinds of ventures, you start subsidizing all manner of things. Why? Because the money is not yours. What does it matter if you win or lose? You have no incentive to save or to do things right: you neither win nor lose. Thus, the essential element of the market economy is missing: the calculation of profits and losses.

If the calculation of profits and losses is missing, we have no human way to guide production: what ought to be produced, how it ought to be produced. Lacking private property, lacking that mechanism of having skin in the game, we have no rational criterion whatsoever, nor do we have the necessary information, for instance, to know whether we should invest more or less in education, more or less in healthcare, more or less in public works, more or less in justice. Because we do not know; we lack the information on which sector society genuinely demands, and the criteria for administering those goods are purely political: they respond to interest group lobbying or to whoever happens to occupy the apparatus or positions of power in that hypothetical structure we call the State. We lack that, and that is the primary issue. We do not know whether we should have more courts or fewer courts. We do not know whether we should have more schools or fewer schools. The criteria are merely quantitative. We do not know whether we should expand La Aurora Airport or downsize it. We do not even know whether a state-owned enterprise makes a profit or runs a loss, because the cost-benefit calculations of public enterprises and organizations are purely accounting figures, not entrepreneurial ones. Any properly funded public company or administration can show a surplus: there is no limit. And conversely: underfund any public enterprise, and it will run a deficit every time. But they are not funded through voluntary contributions; they are funded through political allocations. Whether it runs a deficit or a surplus is merely a matter of the budget assigned to it at any given moment. There is no genuine economic calculation. That is to say, La Aurora Airport took in 10 million quetzales and spent 11: there is an accounting loss. Or a public enterprise took in 12 million quetzales and spent 10: there is an accounting surplus. There is no real profit or loss whatsoever. It simply depends on an initial grant. The profit and loss are purely bookkeeping entries. They are not real. It simply hinges on whether the initial political allocation is sufficient or not to sustain that apparatus. But whether that apparatus itself is the right one, we do not know. Whether the budget allocation we give it is appropriate or not, we do not know either, nor can we know.

The second point we will address here: economic calculation. I have already discussed this with some of you present here, but it applies equally to public organizations. Who among those present can explain the theorem of the impossibility of economic calculation under socialism? How is it that there are no prices? What does the argument consist of?

As you know, criticisms of socialism traditionally focused on the lack of incentives. The classic critique by [Mallock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hurrell_Mallock)^[British novelist and political theorist.], for example, was that socialism cannot work due to a lack of incentives [@mallock1908critical]. Critiques of socialism always followed this line: if everyone earns the same, why work at all if our earnings will be identical anyway? The system is utterly inefficient because nobody works when everyone earns the same. That is the classic argument. Others, such as [Hayek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Hayek)^[Austrian-born British economist, Nobel laureate in Economics.], for instance in *The Road to Serfdom* [@hayek1944road], introduced arguments that the State under socialism must necessarily become tyrannical. If the State controls all means of production—and this argument can also be used as a dysfunction of public administration—if the State controls all means of production in a socialist State, and you want to stage a theatrical play criticizing the political regime, where do you stage it? If you want to broadcast a radio show criticizing the government, where do you broadcast it? If you want to educate your children in different values, whether religious, economic, or moral, where do you educate them? If you want to publish a newspaper, how do you print it? Thus, to the extent that the State monopolizes any social sphere, it simply curtails freedom in that domain. If the State monopolizes education, it controls education, even if it leaves the remaining spheres free. If it controls the monetary system, it eliminates freedom in the use of money: establishing competing currencies, or setting interest rates different from those dictated by the central bank, and so forth. In this respect, we already see a dysfunction of administration: it eliminates liberty via two paths. First, because it forces you to finance it coercively, and by financing it, your own liberty is restricted, because when resources are taken from you, your freedom of action diminishes. Stripping you of resources is stripping you of realms of liberty. From now on, if you were planning to take a trip, you can no longer take it. If you were planning to buy a piece of clothing, you can no longer buy it. If you were planning to buy a certain food, you can no longer afford it, because the State has already seized that resource. Every confiscation of resources via taxation restricts your freedom through that channel, and on the other hand, through the monopoly over service provision. This is the second critique of socialism: socialism as inherently destructive of liberty.

However, the third argument was outlined by [Maximilian Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Weber)^[German sociologist, central figure in the development of sociology.] in a celebrated book entitled *Economy and Society* [@weber1921economy]. There he pointed out the problem of calculation. It was also noted by a prime minister of the Netherlands named [Nicolaas Pierson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaas_Pierson)^[Economist and Prime Minister of the Netherlands.], who began to see what the problem of calculation was. He spoke of how we could trade cheese in a socialist society: how could we trade Dutch round cheeses for German locomotives? At what exchange ratio do they trade, and how? There is an absence of prices. Therefore, how can we establish that ratio? Pierson was among the first to see it. A Russian historian and economist named [Boris Brutzkus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Brutzkus)^[Russian economist.] also raised the problem of calculation after the Soviet revolution was established [@brutzkus1982economic]. But above all, it was [Ludwig von Mises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises)^[Austrian economist, leading figure of the Austrian School of Economics.], who presented the issue in an earlier article and especially in his book *Socialism*, demonstrating the economic impossibility of socialism [@vonmises1922socialism].

This has an extension. His student [Murray Rothbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_Rothbard)^[American economist of the Austrian School.] in *Man, Economy, and State* dedicated a chapter to extending the argument of the impossibility of economic calculation not only to a socialist economy, but to the large corporation or giant firm, arguing that beyond a certain size, a firm cannot calculate either [@rothbard1962man]. That is why under capitalism small firms systematically outmaneuver and consume large firms, and rightly so, contrary to what many of you might think. It is the opposite: the small enterprise plans better, calculates better, compared to the large enterprise, which turns into a dinosaur unable to survive in the market. It is a process of dynamic creation. But that calculation argument can be extended further: it can be extended to empires and, above all, to public policies and public administrations.

Public administrations, as we saw earlier, are partial socialisms. They are socialized spheres of the economy—that is, they lack private property and are therefore unavoidably subject to all the restrictions identified by the theory of economic calculation under socialism. Beyond a certain scale, public enterprises lack prices, lack internal prices, and cannot calculate. When I say they cannot calculate, consider education: how much education should there be? What quality must that education provide? Up to what age should education be provided? Where should schooling take place? These are questions the market resolves effortlessly. The State is incapable. It assigns a price politically. Not a price: it assigns a quantity, a quality, and a service based on political criteria, without any real information.

This is even more obvious in the monetary realm. The world of money, ladies and gentlemen, is it private or is it public? Is the monetary realm socialist or capitalist? What do you think? Who dares to answer? The realm of money. Yes, capitalist? Why? Well, my question to you is: who determines the quantity of money that must exist in the economy? Who determines the price that money must have? Who determines the quality of that money? Consumers? The State? Can you pay with gold and silver here? Can you pay with gold and silver, can you pay with, I don't know, Dutch currency, Swedish currency, say, with crowns? In Guatemala, in what currency must you pay? In quetzales. And why? Because of legal tender laws. That is called forced tender. Each State monopolizes the creation of money. It determines what counts as money and what does not. For instance, it decrees that gold and silver cannot be monetized. It decrees that the only valid currency is the quetzal. Mind you: not only paper quetzales, but bank-created quetzales. When you use a credit card, you transfer money from your account to the merchant's account. Bank credit, bank deposits, enjoy the exact same status as currency. An accounting ledger entry suffices to buy you clothes, food, cars, travel, all kinds of things. That represents a debasement of monetary quality, because a significant portion of that money is created *ex novo*—it is freshly created money—yet the State decrees that this new money is also legal tender, through the bank credit multiplier.

The same applies to education, healthcare, public works. How many highways should there be in Guatemala? How many schools? How many universities, and especially primary schools? How much money should there be in Guatemala? What price should it carry? The central bank also sets the price of money through the discount rate. And how does it know that this price is the correct one? How can it possibly know? It has no information. In the absence of private property, we do not know whether that price is right or wrong. We do not know whether the existing schools, courts, healthcare facilities, or highways are the right ones or not, whether they bear the right cost or not, whether there are too few or too many. Nobody knows. And there lies the principal dysfunction. That is why governments function poorly: because they possess no benchmark by which to determine it. They calculate by imitation, they calculate by memory, and above all, they calculate by politics, according to the pressure of interest groups or powers present in Guatemalan society at any given moment. If a left-wing government is in power, labor unions and certain political actors will exert their pressure for specific ends. If the right governs, other actors will push for different ends. But in either case, the allocation criterion is political, not economic. There is no calculation.

And if calculation works at all, if those sectors function to any degree, it is because the remainder of the economy is not socialized and can therefore shed some light. An educational administration, if it has a benchmark in private schools, knows roughly what schooling might cost. If private universities exist, it knows roughly what higher education costs. If other countries exist in the world, it knows roughly how prices are set for things. Indeed, Soviet communists, to set their prices, took the catalog of an American department store, looked at the prices of goods, and solved their equations with that. Or they relied on black markets to gauge prices, or at least relied on historical memory. Is this reasonably clear?

This is the first argument. Public administration is a socialist entity, a socialist segment of social life, and is therefore subject to all the problems of socialism. The same applies to defense, the same applies to policing, and so on. How much defense should Guatemala have? Does it have too much? Does it have too little? How many police officers does it have? Too many, too few? All classical State functions pose this dilemma, and we have no way of knowing whether we are acting correctly. This is the first point. It is not merely a matter of being efficient or inefficient: it is a problem of calculation. It is therefore a reality that resource allocation in these cases is necessarily distorted, because we lack any market indicator to inform us. Voting is an atrocious indicator for allocating public resources. Consequently, we enter another question, which is yet another effect of socialism: questions of scale and size. What is the correct scale of the State? What is the proper dimension of the State?

The State typically tends to grow, precisely because it lacks market indicators. It does not grow or shrink according to the value of the product it offers on the market. A commercial enterprise, a shop, a department store, grows or contracts, earns greater or lesser profits, depending on whether the product it offers satisfies consumers more or less. In the State, no such dynamic exists, no such mechanism operates. Therefore, the growth process is driven primarily by political factors. The most powerful actors within government seek to expand their sphere of action into civil society, and indeed there is an expansionary tendency inherent to bureaucracy. Problems of interventionism emerge. The State intervenes in ever more social arenas. It intervenes through labor market regulations, through environmental mandates, through historic heritage protections, gradually augmenting its power across all facets of social life. And we see it everywhere. For example, the State loves to control prices. It loves setting prices, removing them, and so forth: the price of bread, the price of staples. It loves legislating on the environment. All of this entails a massive expansion of its authority. It widens its capacity to intervene in those realms and expropriates private property sphere by sphere. Now your private property is no longer fully yours, because before altering it you must conduct an environmental impact study so that your property remains unchanged. Or if you possess some artistic heritage, as Professor Garín was telling me earlier: if you have some artistic heirloom in your house, that artwork is not truly yours—it belongs to the government. If they catalog it, they can seize it under the guise of national interest. And all of this creates an incentive to expand.

Two dynamics explain this mechanism of growth, this bureaucratic imperialism. One is explained by a gentleman named [Parkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Northcote_Parkinson)^[British naval historian and author.], when discussing bureaucracies: the bureaucratic interest is to grow [@parkinson1958law]. If I am a police officer, if I am a bureaucrat, what is the easiest path to promotion, or to acquiring greater power? To have more subordinates, to increase my revenue—on the supply side, as it were. How is that achieved? Quite simply, by expanding the scope of intervention, I suddenly gain new subordinates; and having new subordinates, by virtue of seniority, I secure higher pay and command greater resources.

For instance, the State has a profound interest in criminalizing behavior. Conduct that was historically unrestricted is gradually criminalized by the State, driven by vested interests. For example, in the United States, as people were telling me recently, there is an enormous prison lobby. The United States has hundreds of thousands, millions—over a million inmates. And there is a prison lobby whose livelihood depends on keeping prisons full. If there are few prisoners, their function cannot be justified. Many police departments require high crime rates; otherwise, their funding disappears. And one observes a steady expansion of what is deemed criminal. Take drugs, for instance: up until 1910, you could buy heroin freely. Not only was it sold in any shop, it was advertised in newspapers. Cocaine was advertised widely—even the Pope endorsed cocaine wine, [Vin Mariani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vin_Mariani)^[Tonic wine with coca marketed in the 19th century.]. Promotional posters featured the Pope as an endorsement for consumers! Heroin was used in children's cough syrup and sold everywhere, and likewise with other drugs. In Spain, opium could be bought at any tobacconist, alongside tobacco and everyday items, without the slightest issue. But suddenly someone decided to criminalize it, unleashing a perverse dynamic of criminalizing more and more things, because it never stops. Notice: prohibition did not stop with those drugs from 1910; rather, any newly synthesized substance that rulers decide should be banned is placed on a list, by their decree. The same happens with prostitution, and with a whole host of human behaviors that are progressively criminalized.

And what is in it for them? The first incentive is what I described: an entire industry grows around it, and hundreds of thousands of people make their living from criminalization and the expansion of the State into those areas. Because in the realm of money, in the world of labor, you spawn legions of inspectors, accountants, and controllers dedicated to policing these matters. In tax collection, an entire bureaucracy is created with a vested interest in having as many taxes and complex regulations as possible, so that they may administer them. This is a perverse dynamic of the State—an expansionary dynamic that grows unchecked. We have an interest in having the State intervene in as many things as possible: the more things it controls, the greater my chances of promotion, the more power I yield as a politician, and the faster I rise as a police commissioner or bureaucrat. The more police officers there are, the easier it is for me to be promoted to chief of police, and the easier it is to get a salary raise. That is the first dynamic: bureaucratic expansion.

Second, we touch upon another issue. All State action operates ostensibly in broad daylight, yet aside from these visible "white" benefits, it offers immense black-market rents. The State is an enormous source of illicit rents; State intervention generates vast illegal profits. For example, in many countries around the world, more than 50% of police officers are entangled in drug trafficking. In Spain, during the eras of contraband and drug smuggling, entire police barracks were arrested for ties to the drug trade. Many police officers in numerous countries have been involved in prostitution rackets or human trafficking rings. Typically, those who protect brothels in many parts of the world are police officers. Those who shield drug traffickers in many corners of the globe are police officers. I am not saying all police officers engage in this, but it constitutes a massive source of income for politicians and bureaucrats, because rents can be extracted from one side and privileges granted on the other. Not everyone, obviously, but it is undeniably an engine of profit. In fact, who are the fiercest opponents of decriminalizing these activities? The cartels and their allies within government. In every administration, within police forces and bureaucracies, they are the primary opponents, because legalizing them destroys their business model.

So there we have it outlined. This is explained by [Bruce Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_L._Benson)^[American economist.] in a book entitled *The Enterprise of Law: Justice Without a State* [@benson1990enterprise]. Obviously, I am not painting all politicians with the same brush. But that corrupt actors exist and do these things—yes, we all know it. It does not mean all of them are corrupt, but corrupt actors certainly exist. And these individuals have a direct stake in State expansion. In environmental policy, in all these arenas, the same logic applies. The inevitable consequence of what I am describing is the phenomenon of corruption.

What causes corruption? Who dares to say? Where does corruption flourish? Pardon? Where there is money? No. Where then? What did I hear up there? Where there are restrictions. Where something is regulated or limited by the State. Is there a black market or corruption in the market for ballpoint pens? Is there corruption in the market for sugar or saccharin? Where does corruption thrive? Where the money is, as you say? Where the business is? In which sectors is there corruption? In urban planning and zoning, for example. Can you build a house wherever you please, as tall as you please, in whatever color and style you please? No. And what does that mean? That to build a house, what do you need? A permit. And therefore that permit is worth money, yes or no? And where money is at stake, an incentive for corruption immediately appears. Indeed, in my country, the most corrupt politicians are systematically found in urban planning, where a politician's signature is worth cold hard cash. Corruption emerges in any sector subject to intervention, because if someone wishes to pursue an activity and an official blocks them, they will calculate whether it pays to bribe the politician or bureaucrat to get it done. The more regulated and intervened an economy is, the more corruption will flourish.

The same occurs with mafias. Mafias simply step in to supply an area that has been prohibited. Where do mafias operate, for example, in the United States? In teddy bears, in pencils, in bottled water? Where is the mafia? What does the mafia do? What goods does it buy and sell? Arms, why? Because they are restricted. What else? Drugs. And what is peculiar about drugs? A drug is a chemical compound like any other. Any moderately equipped factory can manufacture any drug. Any competent chemist can produce a drug. What is the problem with drugs? They are prohibited. Yet people, despite the ban, continue to demand drugs. And because demand persists, the mafia emerges to supply them. The same with gambling, or whatever other goods happen to be banned. In Cuba, for instance, people told me there was a thriving black market in condensed milk, which was even used as a medium of exchange. Being a State monopoly that you could not buy freely, it became traded on the black market. Black markets trade in any good whatsoever, provided it is banned. Or do you think that in Venezuela today there are no black markets for bread, cooking oil, or basic necessities? When prices are price-controlled, black markets inevitably spring up for those goods. And I am certain that if you impose price controls on any good here, or regulate it heavily, you will generate a black market *ipso facto*.

Therefore, you must analyze corruption through this lens. Corruption stems fundamentally from a lack of secure property rights and an excess of State intervention in a specific domain of social life. Whenever you ban something, you will spawn some form of black market or corruption. And this is a perverse dynamic of the State. People often blame markets for corruption. No: corruption is the consequence of the absence of markets. This is an element we can elaborate on later if you wish.

A third problem of State intervention, among those we flagged at the outset, is encapsulated in a couple of insights that the late [Aaron Wildavsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Wildavsky)^[American political scientist.] explained in a celebrated book entitled *Speaking Truth to Power: The Art and Craft of Policy Analysis* [@wildavsky1979speaking]. He observed: in the public sector, a curious paradox, a perverse dynamic arises: the worse things are, the better they get funded. Take my home city, for example. I come from Santiago de Compostela; I am Galician. A few years ago, if I recall correctly, a ranking showed that among cities of its size (100,000 inhabitants), my city ranked as the safest in all of Spain by number of crimes and assaults. It was the safest city in Spain. In another ranking, if memory serves, Seville or Valencia—let's say Valencia—ranked as having the highest crime rate per 1,000 residents. Now, my question to you is: what reward did the police officers of Santiago receive for performing so well? Presumably the police had something to do with the outcome. Public services, contrary to popular belief, are not uniform everywhere. There are good public universities and bad ones. There are good police forces and bad ones. There are good doctors and bad ones, all within the public sector. Even within the public realm, quality varies. It is inferior to the private sector, but variations exist. Now then, what reward did the Santiago police get for performing well, and what punishment did the Valencia police receive for performing so poorly? Who dares answer? What reward did my city's police get? Precisely: their budget was cut and their personnel reduced! They said: "They're doing well; we don't need to spend so much on policing there." And what horrific punishment was inflicted on the failing department? A larger budget and more officers! If a public university or hospital functions smoothly, if people don't complain and it operates within cost constraints, frugally, what reward does it get? Budget cuts. But if an institution functions disastrously, because it is managed by political criteria, the well-behaved one gets ignored, while the squeaky wheel gets the grease.

[Albert O. Hirschman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_O._Hirschman)^[American economist, political scientist, and sociologist.] wrote a book called *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty* [@hirschman1970exit]. The market operates via exit. That is, if I dislike a shop, I leave and that is the end of it. I never walk back in. It functions through exit, cleanly. There is no conflict. If we are mistreated in a store, we say good day and never return. We naturally rely on the exit mechanism. In the State, no exit mechanism is available. Whether you like the service or not, you are forced to pay for it. In many cases you must pay for public schooling: even if you pay for a private university, you must finance public education for others. Furthermore, if the State holds a monopoly—in justice, for example—if you dislike their courts, where do you go? You have nowhere to go. So what happens in the public sector? The mechanism used is voice, as Hirschman explains: riots, protests, demonstrations, and political agitation. Because government, as I have explained many times, is force—pure force. And being pure force, government does not respond to economic arguments; it responds only to force and political pressure. If a public service malfunctions—the police or a hospital—people protest, demonstrate, exert political pressure, demand their rights; and the government, sensitive to noise, deprives the quiet sector to feed the disruptive one. This is a thoroughly perverse incentive, in stark contrast to the market. In the market, when a sector operates efficiently, others imitate it, and resources, driven by profit and loss, flow from failing sectors toward thriving ones. In the public sector, the reverse happens: resources flow from where things work best toward where they fail most miserably.

And there is yet another perverse incentive, Wildavsky explains: problems shine brightest when they are smallest and on the verge of disappearing. Consequently, priorities become distorted. What do I mean? When was there more hunger in the world: now, or in the past? In the past. There has never been less hunger in the world than today. There has never been less illiteracy in the world than today. There has never been less abuse against women—and note carefully what I am saying—than today. I am acutely aware of what I am saying, and I know it remains a serious problem in your country, as in all countries. Yet, as grave as it is, it has diminished drastically compared to, say, a century ago. But what happens? In politics, a problem captures the spotlight precisely when it shrinks to a manageable scale. This lack of perspective causes us to neglect massive ongoing problems while fixating on issues that capture headlines. This does not mean it isn't a problem—of course it is a grave problem. My point is that the spotlight shines brightest when the abuse is least widespread, not when it was universally tolerated. Tragically, in Spain two centuries ago, killing a woman was not even classified as a distinct felony under many jurisdictions. Today, thank God, it is criminalized and prosecuted. But it can be actively prosecuted precisely because it has become an aberration rather than the norm. Just as illiteracy can be combated because it has shrunk, and hunger can be tackled because absolute poverty has plummeted. While this focus has a certain logic, it leads to neglecting other deep-seated social issues and distorts our assessment of reality. Problems shine when they are smallest, which often leads people to believe that things have never been worse, when in fact we have never been better off.

With that, I will open the floor to discussion, as I see my allotted 45 minutes have elapsed. Now, if you wish, I would be delighted to answer any questions, debate with anyone who disagrees with what I've presented, or elaborate on any topic. Let's see what kind of students the EPRI has. I want to see how Edu educates his pupils! That is what I came here for: to see if you have been well trained. Let's go, speak up—otherwise you will make these gentlemen look bad, and I will tease Edu afterwards! What kind of school of politics is this—a department of political science, or a sewing and dressmaking academy?

### Question: "What do you think of the 1929 crash and how Roosevelt, through the New Deal, brought the United States out of the crisis?" {.unnumbered}

[Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt)^[President of the United States from 1933 to 1945.] did not pull the country out of the crisis. Roosevelt turned a relatively brief recession into a twelve-year Great Depression, precisely through such interventions, and the United States did not fully emerge from the Depression until after the World War. If you look closely, the public policies implemented were what aggravated the crisis. In a crisis of that nature, the correct course is to do nothing. Compare the crisis of 1929 with the crisis of 1920. Are you familiar with 1920? What happened? There were two near-consecutive crises, in 1920 and in 1929. We only study the 1929 crash because it dragged on endlessly. The 1920 crisis was sharper, yet nobody remembers it because it corrected itself in months. In a crisis, what needs to be done is nothing. Assets must be allowed to liquidate, unviable firms must go bankrupt, banks must fail, prices must adjust and deflate, and a healthy recovery can then take root on sound principles.

Roosevelt's administration did not follow *laissez-faire* policies. It began implementing what are now called "stimulus packages." Even before [Keynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Maynard_Keynes)^[British economist.], Roosevelt was already doing it, and it accomplished nothing, because it *can* accomplish nothing. The economy needs to heal and readjust, and stimulus measures simply squandered scarce remaining capital propping up bankrupt enterprises.

Are you familiar with the Austrian theory of the business cycle? If not, read Hayek on the subject, or Mises's pioneering work *The Theory of Money and Credit* [@vonmises1912money], or Lionel Robbins's book on the Great Depression [@robbins1934depression], or Murray Rothbard's *America's Great Depression* [@rothbard1963depression]. Today, schools rarely teach this perspective. For us, the crisis is precisely an error of calculation—economic calculation. The State does not know what price to assign to money and artificially suppresses interest rates. Despite what [Milton Friedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Friedman)^[American economist, Nobel laureate in Economics.] and [Anna Schwartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Schwartz)^[American economist, co-author of A Monetary History of the United States.] argue in *A Monetary History of the United States*, an enormous credit expansion took place during the 1920s, which their metrics mischaracterized [@friedman1963monetary]. Interest rates were artificially suppressed.

Why is the interest rate so crucial? The interest rate is a market price that conveys vital information. What does a high interest rate tell you? It tells you: capital is scarce. You cannot afford to embark on long-term investments. You cannot buy new machinery, you cannot build new factories, you cannot buy that luxury car, you cannot expand your home. Why? Because the savings are not there. How do we know they are not there? By the high interest rate. A low interest rate tells you the exact opposite: savings abound, you can expand productive activity, purchase new equipment, buy an automobile, remodel your house. That is how a free market coordinates time. But when the State fixes the price of money and depresses it artificially, what happens? Widespread malinvestment occurs. People begin buying tractors, building houses, and purchasing assets they cannot realistically finance. Eventually reality reasserts itself, and a wave of bankruptcies follows. Those bankruptcies consume capital. Following the crash, that economy is 20% or 25% poorer. The proper remedy is to let wages adjust, let prices deflate, allow insolvent industries to fail without sinking another quetzal into them, and let recovery begin from a lower base, reaching full employment and sound sustainable growth. Instead, governments attempt to bail out failing companies and insolvent banks, consuming scarce remaining capital to prop up doomed operations. And that is what prolongs the depression.

What has been happening with the European crisis? It has dragged on for years with no end in sight, precisely because authorities do everything possible to block market adjustments through Keynesian interventions.

### Question: "Regarding national security, which is a state monopoly, would you recommend privatizing the military and police?" {.unnumbered}

Security was historically private, young lady. The notion that the central state must monopolize defense belongs only to the theory of the modern State, where consolidating power at the center was paramount. Consider: what were Roman legions—state bureaucracies or mercenaries? Mercenaries. The troops who fought across Europe, or even those who arrived in the Americas—what were they? Mercenaries. What percentage of modern intelligence and surveillance work is private versus public? Roughly 70% is private contractors. There is nothing bizarre about private defense; historically, it was the norm. El Cid Campeador—have you heard of him? El Cid was a mercenary commander who even fought in the service of Muslim rulers. Defense and policing were historically private. They functioned far more effectively and were infinitely less destructive, far less criminal, than the standing armies of the State.

Consider privateers. Privateers were effective private naval combatants. A privateer was simply a private ship owner; the State granted a letter of marque, and you set sail to battle the English or raid opposing merchant vessels. It was a business enterprise; there was no need to establish an enormous naval bureaucracy. And as a mercenary or privateer, you had every incentive to minimize bloodshed, because mercenaries killed far fewer people than national conscript armies ever did.

### Question: "There are roughly 150,000 private security guards and 39,000 police officers, yet insecurity remains high and illegal armed groups exist. Does this really suggest security should be private?" {.unnumbered}

Let's begin there. Private security flourishes here, likely because Guatemala emerged from an extended civil conflict: there is a demographic stratum of thousands of individuals accustomed to combat. It is, generally speaking, a society with higher baseline violence than others. As a consequence, people demand far more security. The demand reflects the environment, not whether private security is inherently flawed. Why do people demand so much security here compared to other countries?

You seem to start from the premise that the state police is legitimate and good, while private security is suspect—one is legal, the other illicit. Why must that be so? I do not see it. Furthermore, you invoked a concept I sought to criticize in this lecture: an "efficient" amount of security. How can that possibly be determined? Efficiency is an engineering concept applicable to a diesel engine: so many liters of fuel for so many horsepower—that is efficiency. A locomotive can be efficient. But public security can never be called "efficient," because there is no single metric, no objective benchmark. To take an extreme example: if I execute or imprison every young male between the ages of 15 and 25, crime would drop precipitously, would it not? You would virtually eradicate street crime, because that demographic commits the vast majority of offenses. But would that be efficient? No, it would be an immense injustice. Other values compete with it. That would be the most expeditious way to suppress crime, but would it be socially desirable or horrifyingly unjust? Efficiency is a physical concept improperly transposed into social science. You cannot speak of an "efficient policy"—efficient for whom? That is the crux of the matter.

### Question: "The State bans many behaviors by top-down decrees without considering social reality. What should be done about existing crime, and what is the alternative to monopolizing security without spawning more criminality?" {.unnumbered}

You raise a fascinating point: to what extent is an act a crime in itself, versus a crime manufactured by the State? I do not have local statistics at hand, but in European and American prisons, roughly 80% of inmates are incarcerated for victimless offenses—acts that under any natural law ethical framework would not constitute a crime at all. Inmates are overwhelmingly locked up for drugs, gambling, or prostitution, which across history were standard commercial activities. In this respect, the law creates the crime, not the other way around. The law defines harmless conduct as criminal. For instance, I was told that in Guatemala you can face jail time for smoking in certain areas. That strikes me as utterly absurd: criminalizing smoking in designated places, turning statutory law into a confiscatory apparatus. Is that natural law, or is it a decree where the State invents a crime?

The Swedish economic historian [Eli Heckscher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Heckscher) recounts in his classic study *Mercantilism* that thousands of people were executed in Britain for buying and selling contraband textiles [@heckscher1935mercantilism]. The Crown maintained a monopoly on certain textiles, such as [calico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calico)^[Cotton fabric, often printed.], prohibiting imports of cheaper or higher-quality foreign fabrics. Anyone caught with forbidden cloth was executed as a smuggler. Were those people criminals? They were criminals solely because the State decreed it, not because their actions were inherently immoral. They were peacefully buying and selling cloth without harming anyone, yet the State declared their trade illicit to protect favored domestic guilds.

How do we break the monopoly? By abolishing it. Anarchism. I am what people call an "ancap"—an anarcho-capitalist. I suspect there might be a few of us in this room as well!

### Question: "Wouldn't eliminating the State simply restore people's freedom to exert violence at will?" {.unnumbered}

Look, the comparison is stark: during the twentieth century, States murdered hundreds of millions of people. Estimates suggest that in the twentieth century, between 250 and 300 million people were slaughtered by their own governments through wars, democide, and purges. Private homicides during that same span amounted to perhaps 25 million—a ratio of ten to one. Yet people repeat the thesis, championed by [John Stuart Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stuart_Mill)^[British philosopher and political economist.] in *Considerations on Representative Government* [@mill1861representative], that the State is an indispensable engine of civilization. Consider: a shepherd watches over his sheep so they do not fight among themselves, and a farmer ensures his chickens do not peck each other to death. Why does the shepherd protect the sheep from the wolf, or from rival shepherds? Because he does not want another predator eating his flock, and he does not want the sheep killing one another. Who bears the loss? He does. Of course he wants peace! The calmer the flock, the more wool he can shear. If the sheep slaughtered each other, there would be little wealth for the shepherd to extract. Of course he desires peace. But I doubt the sheep heading to the slaughterhouse is thrilled about having lived peacefully with the flock. It is a stark metaphor, but historically accurate.

The predatory theory of the State runs along these lines. You might object: "Doesn't that return us to a state where only those with resources can defend themselves?" Well, what resources do you have against the State today? In theory, constitutional human rights. And if the State chooses to violate them, who punishes it? Who holds it accountable? Can an individual in this room, out of sheer whim, employ physical coercion to seize whatever he wants from the rest of you? No, because individuals in this room possess ample means to defend themselves, arm themselves, or form alliances against an aggressor. A private monopoly of violence is extraordinarily difficult to establish. Conversely, a single armed police officer can walk in here and arrest all of us without anyone resisting. Two armed men can march us out. Who, then, represents the greater threat?

[John Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke)^[English philosopher.] put it brilliantly: to escape the mischiefs of polecats and foxes, men surrender themselves to the jaws of a lion. The polecats and foxes are our unruly neighbors who annoy us; and to shield ourselves from them, we deliver ourselves into the paws of a lion that can devour us with impunity. The State, I repeat, does not exist as an independent entity; it is a necessary myth designed to ensure that you pay taxes and comply without resistance, denying the possibility of human cooperation outside coercion.

### Question: "Why would the State be more powerful, as an apparatus of dominion, than the individual?" {.unnumbered}

The State takes great care to monopolize violence—to remain the sole wielder of organized force within a territory. To achieve this, in many countries it disarms the population, tolerating only its own armed agents so that no one can defy it. Hayek included a chapter in *The Road to Serfdom* entitled "Why the Worst Get on Top" [@hayek1944road]. In politics, in the apparatus of the State, the most ruthless and skilled power-seekers naturally rise to the apex. Thus, to rid ourselves of the nuisance of our neighbors, we fall into the clutches of the most unscrupulous actors. To protect ourselves from petty disputes, we grant a monopoly on violence to a single entity. I fail to see the logic in that trade-off.

Why, then, do people to this day seek shelter in the State, and why are there no fully anarchist societies where men govern themselves peacefully? Quite simply: because they are not permitted to. You all attended school, I presume. You did not study at home; you went to school. Is schooling mandatory in Guatemala? On paper, yes. But consider the content of that education: what did you study there? History. History of what? History of the State. Did you study how seventeenth-century Guatemalans lived, what they ate, how they farmed? No: you studied the presidents of Guatemala, the battles of the State. You studied the history of the State! Geography: what is geography? Rivers, mountains, borders. Whose borders? Guatemala's—the geography of the State! Geography is perhaps the most manipulative subject taught in schools. Language: what language do you speak? The language of the State. Why Castilian Spanish, and not Persian? Because it is the official tongue of the State. What do you learn in schools? Civic education—the ethics of obedience to the State. The curriculum is engineered to mold obedient citizens, not to teach practical skills. You are not taught how to trade, how to start a business, how to repair an engine. You learn what the State wants you to learn, designed to manufacture political compliance.

The geometry you were taught originated with Egyptian priests calculating land surface areas to levy taxes upon the harvest. Furthermore, the State assigns you a national registry number, names, surnames, and an official address, ensuring that it can locate, tax, and conscript you at will.

Professor Santiago is signaling me that time is up. It has been a pleasure.
